draft.title: Biogeography and embryology as evidence
card: the study of where species live. Related species are often found in nearby places, as if they spread from a shared ancestor.
Most marsupials live in Australia and nearby New Guinea. Their common ancestors lived there, and they changed into many species, such as kangaroos and koalas.
the study of embryos, the earliest stages of an animal's growth. Fish, birds and humans look very alike as early embryos, though the adults differ greatly.
These similar early embryos are evidence that all vertebrates, animals with backbones, share common ancestors. Both kinds of evidence support evolution.
draft.remember: Related species living close together and similar early embryos both point to shared ancestors.

a.q: Early embryos of a fish, a bird and a human look very similar. What does this suggest?
opts: They will grow into the same animal
They live in the same place
They are all the same species
a.why: Similar early development suggests the animals inherited it from a common ancestor. It does not mean they become the same animal, since the adults are very different.
a.clue: Think about what similar features inherited from the past suggest.

b.q: Many species of finch live on a group of islands off South America. They look similar to a finch on the nearby mainland, but not to finches on distant continents. What is the best explanation?
opts: They descended from a shared ancestor from the mainland
Each species began separately on its own island
They changed because the islands are warm
Finches cannot be related to species on other continents
b.why: Close relatives living in nearby places fit descent from a shared ancestor that spread from the mainland. Separate starts would not explain the similarity to the mainland finch.
b.clue: Why would close relatives live close together?

b.best: They descended from a shared ancestor from the mainland
